questions.prompt: Sodium hydroxide solution is added to a solution of an unknown salt and gives a pale blue precipitate that does not dissolve in excess. The cation is
questions.explanation: Copper(II) hydroxide is pale blue and insoluble in excess alkali. Fe2+ gives a green precipitate, and Zn2+ and Al3+ give white precipitates that dissolve. Fe3+ gives a red-brown precipitate, not a pale blue one.

questions.prompt: Excess aqueous ammonia is added to a solution containing Cu2+ ions. The result is
questions.explanation: The precipitate first formed redissolves, forming the complex [Cu(NH3)4]2+, which is deep blue.

questions.prompt: A green precipitate that turns brown on standing in air forms when sodium hydroxide is added to a solution. The cation is
questions.explanation: Iron(II) hydroxide is green and is slowly oxidised by air to brown iron(III) hydroxide. Fe3+ gives a reddish-brown precipitate immediately. Cu2+ gives a pale blue precipitate, and Ca2+ gives at most a faint white one.

questions.prompt: A reddish-brown precipitate is formed with sodium hydroxide solution. The cation is
questions.explanation: Iron(III) hydroxide is reddish-brown. Fe2+ is the nearest wrong option because it gives a green precipitate.

questions.prompt: A white precipitate forms with sodium hydroxide, dissolves in excess sodium hydroxide, and also dissolves in excess ammonia. The cation is
questions.explanation: Zinc hydroxide dissolves in both excess alkali and excess ammonia. Al3+ dissolves in excess NaOH but not in excess NH3, and that difference distinguishes the two.

questions.prompt: A white precipitate dissolves in excess sodium hydroxide but not in excess ammonia solution. The cation is
questions.explanation: Aluminium hydroxide is amphoteric and dissolves in excess alkali, but it does not form an ammine complex. Zn2+ is the nearest wrong choice because it dissolves in both.

questions.prompt: A solution gives a white precipitate with sodium hydroxide that dissolves in excess, and a yellow precipitate with potassium iodide. The cation is
questions.explanation: Lead(II) iodide is bright yellow, which separates Pb2+ from Zn2+ and Al3+. Both of those have white precipitates, but their iodides are soluble.

questions.prompt: A white precipitate forms with sodium hydroxide and does not dissolve in excess. The salt gives a brick-red flame. The cation is
questions.explanation: Calcium hydroxide is a white precipitate insoluble in excess, and calcium gives a brick-red flame. Mg2+ behaves the same way with NaOH but gives no flame colour.

questions.prompt: A solution is acidified with dilute nitric acid and silver nitrate is added. A white precipitate that dissolves in dilute ammonia solution indicates
questions.explanation: Silver chloride is white and soluble in dilute ammonia. Silver iodide is yellow and insoluble in dilute ammonia.

questions.prompt: Barium chloride solution is added to a solution acidified with dilute hydrochloric acid, producing a white precipitate that stays. The anion is
questions.explanation: Barium sulphate is insoluble even in acid. Barium carbonate would also be white, but it dissolves in acid, which is why the solution is acidified first.

questions.prompt: Dilute acid is added to a solid, and a gas that turns limewater milky is given off. The solid is most likely a
questions.explanation: Carbonates release carbon dioxide on reaction with acid. Sulphates and chlorides do not give a gas with dilute acid.

questions.prompt: The brown ring test is used to detect
questions.explanation: Freshly prepared iron(II) sulphate and concentrated sulphuric acid, added carefully down the tube, give a brown ring at the junction when nitrate is present.

questions.prompt: An organic liquid decolourises bromine water immediately in the cold. The liquid probably contains
questions.explanation: Alkenes undergo addition with bromine, which removes the brown colour. Alkanes need ultraviolet light and react by substitution. A compound with only single bonds does not decolourise bromine water in the dark, and alcohol and carboxylic acid groups do not react with it in the cold.

questions.prompt: Tollens' reagent gives a silver mirror when warmed with
questions.explanation: Aldehydes are easily oxidised and reduce silver ions to silver. Ketones, the nearest wrong choice, are not oxidised under these conditions.

questions.prompt: Fehling's solution can be used to distinguish
questions.explanation: A brick-red precipitate of copper(I) oxide forms with an aldehyde, but not with a ketone.

questions.prompt: An orange precipitate forms when 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine is added to an organic compound. The compound contains a

options.text: carbonyl group (C=O) of an aldehyde or ketone
double bond between two carbon atoms

questions.explanation: The reagent forms a coloured hydrazone with both aldehydes and ketones, so it shows a carbonyl group but does not separate the two types.

questions.prompt: The enthalpy change of neutralisation for a strong acid and a strong base is approximately

options.text: 57 kJ released per mole of water formed
57 kJ absorbed per mole of water formed
570 kJ released per mole of water formed

questions.explanation: The reaction H+ + OH- -> H2O is exothermic, so heat is released, and the value is close to 57 kJ per mole. An absorbed value would imply an endothermic process, and the solution would cool.

questions.prompt: A pure organic solid is distinguished from an impure sample by its melting point, because impurities

options.text: have no effect on the melting point
lower the melting point and make it melt over a range

questions.explanation: A pure compound melts sharply at a fixed temperature. Impurities disrupt the crystal lattice, so the solid melts lower and over a range.

questions.prompt: In recrystallisation, the crude solid is dissolved in the minimum volume of hot solvent so that

options.text: the solution is saturated and crystals form on cooling

questions.explanation: Using little solvent gives a saturated solution, so the pure compound crystallises as it cools and most impurities stay dissolved.

questions.prompt: When warmed with acidified potassium dichromate(VI), ethanol changes the colour of the mixture from
questions.explanation: The orange dichromate(VI) ion is reduced to green chromium(III) while the alcohol is oxidised. A tertiary alcohol would show no change.
